Modern.brandDescription: Ten Frames is an early-numeracy app for ages 3–7 built entirely on the manipulative that math educators trust most. Modern.industrySummary: Early-math anxiety is the new early-literacy crisis: 2025 NAEP data shows fourth-grade math scores still below pre-pandemic levels, and parent spending on math apps has doubled since 2022. Modern.tagline: Assessment that works like a studio.
Modern.brandDescription: Crit Room is a portfolio-assessment platform for creative education — design schools, bootcamps, and art departments — that replaces rubric spreadsheets with the structured critique. In Crit Room, students pin work, cohorts respond within instructor-set critique frames, and assessment emerges from documented dialogue rather than a single grade. Accreditation-ready records fall out automatically.
Modern.brandNameRationale: The crit — the ritual critique session where work is pinned up and discussed — is the pedagogical heart of every art and design school. The brand names the room where creative judgment is actually formed.
Modern.industrySummary: Creative-education assessment is in quiet crisis in 2026: accreditors demand documented outcomes while studio faculty rightly resist reducing craft to rubric checkboxes. Meanwhile portfolio platforms optimized for job-hunting (not learning) dominate student habits. Tools that capture critique as assessment evidence — satisfying both accreditors and studio culture — are a genuine white space.
Modern.competitorLandscape: Seesaw (seesaw.com) owns K-12 portfolio sharing. Instructure's Canvas (instructure.com) holds the LMS layer with bolt-on portfolios. Behance (behance.net) is where finished work goes to be seen, not assessed. None structure the critique itself — Crit Room's entire product.
Modern.positioningStatement: The only assessment tool built on how studios actually judge work.
Modern.positioningRationale: Faculty adopt tools that respect studio culture; administrators adopt tools that produce accreditation evidence. Crit Room is the rare product both can champion, which is how education software actually spreads.

targetAudience.primary: Design and art faculty 30–60 at degree programs and serious bootcamps, plus the program directors who answer to accreditors. Faculty are tool-skeptical and rubric-averse; directors are drowning in outcome-documentation requests.

Then the software arrived and asked us to translate all of that into a dropdown. We refuse. Crit Room starts from the room: the work, the voices around it, the judgment that forms between them. The paperwork can be a byproduct. The crit cannot.

Creative.brandDescription: The Field Trip Co designs and runs experiential learning days for schools and families — the tide pool, the printing press, the courtroom, the commercial kitchen — each built with a real curriculum spine and zero worksheets. Creative.industrySummary: Experiential learning is rebounding hard post-pandemic: field-trip spending recovered past 2019 levels in 2025, microschools and homeschool co-ops (now serving over 2M US kids) buy experiences instead of buildings, and districts under engagement pressure are re-funding the trips they cut. Creative.tagline: The answer was never the point.
Creative.brandDescription: Show Your Work is a classroom platform where students submit their thinking, not just their answers — voice notes, photographed scratch paper, draft timelines, revision histories. Show Your Work gives teachers a feed of process, tools to comment on reasoning, and portfolios that make growth visible to families. It grades journeys in a world that only ever graded destinations.
Creative.brandNameRationale: 'Show your work' is the most repeated instruction in schooling — scribbled on a million math tests. The platform takes the command literally and builds the infrastructure it always deserved.
Creative.industrySummary: AI answer-generation broke answer-grading: since 2023, any take-home answer can be synthetic, pushing assessment toward process evidence — drafts, reasoning, revision. Process-portfolio pedagogy, long championed in writing and math education, suddenly has an existential tailwind, and districts are actively procuring 'AI-resilient assessment' tools in 2025–26.
Creative.competitorLandscape: Seesaw (seesaw.com) owns elementary portfolio sharing. Padlet (padlet.com) leads flexible boards. ClassDojo (classdojo.com) dominates family communication. All capture artifacts; Show Your Work is built around process capture — the draft trail is the data model.
Creative.positioningStatement: The platform that makes thinking visible — and ungameable.
Creative.positioningRationale: In the AI era, process evidence is the only assessment that proves a human learned. Owning 'show your work' — the phrase every teacher already says — makes the pedagogy shift feel like common sense, not adoption.

targetAudience.primary: Middle and high school teachers 25–55, math and writing first, in districts wrestling with AI policy. Pedagogically ambitious, tool-weary, looking for something that changes what students do rather than what teachers monitor.

Creative.mission: Make the process the product of school.

Creative.manifesto: For a hundred years school asked for the answer and threw away the thinking. Then the machines learned to make answers by the billion, and the answer became worthless overnight. Good. The answer was never the point. The crossed-out line, the second try, the voice note at 11pm saying 'wait, I think I get it' — that was always the education. We built Show Your Work because the scratch paper was the real transcript all along. Keep the drafts. Grade the journey. The destination can prove nothing anymore.

Creative.brandDescription: The Substitute is a staffing and training company that turns the most dreaded slot in schooling into its happiest accident. Creative.brandNameRationale: The substitute teacher is education's most maligned role — the punchline of every sitcom classroom. Naming the company after the role, with a definite article, dares to make it a title worth wanting.
Creative.industrySummary: The substitute shortage became structural after 2020: national fill rates still hover near 80%, meaning millions of instructional hours yearly land on unprepared coverage. Districts outsource to staffing firms competing purely on volume, while sub training remains a 40-minute compliance video. Quality — not headcount — is the unclaimed position in 2025–26.

ESS (ess.com) dominates the southeast. All sell coverage; The Substitute sells the day itself — trained delivery, measured by repeat requests.
Creative.positioningRationale: Districts buy fill rates until a principal experiences a sub who left the class better than they found it — then they buy names. Publishing per-sub repeat-request rates makes quality legible in a volume market.
